17 
Q. 
Please explain how the corrections and updates are organized. 
18 
A. 
The exhibits submitted in this filing show corrections and/or updates and 
19 
indicate the change from the original filing.  The exhibits are labeled with 
20 
“CU” after the original label.  For example, Exhibit __ (RRP-1) in the July 31 
21 
filing is the Statement of Operating Income.  The exhibit showing the 
22 
corrections and/or updates to the Statement of Operating Income is labeled 
23 
Exhibit ___ (RRP-1CU).  The first page of each exhibit provides a summary 
24 
of all adjustments made and reflected in that exhibit.  This summary, or lead 
25 
page, is identified as “Corrections and Updates” under each exhibit number.  
26 
The revised schedules and pages supporting each exhibit correspond to the 
27 
schedules and pages originally filed.  The Company has only included 
28 
exhibits, summaries, schedules, and pages where corrections and/or updates 
29 


--- Page 5 ---
 
Corrections and Updates Testimony of The Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 3 of 40 
 
were made, except for the Exhibit____(RRP-3) schedules, whereby all 
1 
schedules are being included for completeness and readability.   
2 
 
3 
The information requests referenced in the Panel’s testimony are included in 
4 
the workpapers in Exhibit ___ (RRP-11CU) and correspond to the specific 
5 
exhibits and schedules where the corrections and/or updates were made.  For 
6 
example, if a correction and/or update is shown in Exhibit ___ (RRP-3CU), 
7 
Schedule 2 based on a response to an information request, that information 
8 
request is included in the workpapers supporting Exhibit ___ (RRP-3CU), 
9 
Schedule 2.  Where the attachments to information requests are voluminous, 
10 
the Company included only the written response and relevant attachments.

Schedule 1 – Consultant Expense 
13 
Schedule 1 reflects two adjustments to consultant expense.  The first 
14

15

17 
expenses in Schedule 29 and proposed to amortize the total forecast associated 
18 
with rate case legal consultant expenses over the term of the rate plan.  The 
19 
second adjustment reflects the effects of the updated inflation factor to 
20 
consultant expense.

Schedule 2 – Contractor Expense 
1 
Schedule 2 reflects three adjustments to contractor expense.  As explained in 
2 
the response to Information Request No. DPS-525 (Supplemental 1), the 
3 
Company performed an analysis of storm costs that resulted in the need to re-
4 
characterize $4.011 million in minor storms as major deferrable and major 
5 
non-deferrable storm costs.  Because the Company is proposing to change the 
6 
definition of deferrable storms and include both major deferrable and major 
7 
non-deferrable storm costs in the deferral in the Rate Year, the contractor 
8 
costs that have been recategorized from minor storms to major storms needs to 
9 
be normalized.  The first and second adjustments shown in Schedule 2 are the 
10 
change in normalizations to contractor costs resulting from this 
11 
recategorization of minor storm costs.  Specifically, the first adjustment has 
12 
two components and is shown on Exhibit __ (RRP-11), Workpapers to Exhibit 
13 
RRP-3, Schedule 2, Workpaper 2: 
14 
(i) 
The first component of the adjustment reflects the recategorization 
15 
described above that moved contractor costs from minor storms to 
16 
major non-deferrable storm costs and normalizes them out of 
17 
contractor expense.  
18 
(ii) 
The second component of the adjustment relates to the major non-
19 
deferrable storm labor costs, which were normalized out of contractor 
20 
expense in the Company’s July 31 filing, and are now normalized in 
21 


--- Page 10 ---
 
Corrections and Updates Testimony of The Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 8 of 40 
 
Exhibit___(RRP-3), Schedule 23, resulting in a decrease in the amount 
1 
of contractor costs to be normalized. 
2 
The second adjustment also relates to the recategorization described above.  
3 
Specifically, the adjustment is to normalize out of contractors the increase in 
4 
contractor costs resulting from the recategorization of minor storms to major 
5 
deferrable storm costs, as presented on Exhibit __ (RRP-11), Workpapers to 
6 
Exhibit RRP-3, Schedule 2, Workpaper 3.  The third adjustment updates the 
7 
inflation rate.

Schedule 9 – Service Company Rent Expense 
16 
Schedule 9 reflects six adjustments to Service Company rent expense.   
17 
 
18 
The first adjustment was made to update the Long-Term Debt Cost rate from 
19 
4.29 percent to 3.25 percent to align with the Capital Structure Panel’s direct 
20 


--- Page 11 ---
 
Corrections and Updates Testimony of The Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 9 of 40 
 
testimony, as discussed in the Company’s response to Information Request 
1 
No. DPS-485.     
2 
 
3 
The second adjustment updates the Information Technology (“IT”) Existing 
4 
IT Projects MACRS Table to correct a calculation error.  This error was found 
5 
only within the IT Existing Projects model on the MACRS Table tab where 
6 
the calculation for year four inaccurately retained year three’s MACRS rate of 
7 
92.59 percent.  The rate for year four was corrected to 100 percent. 
8 
 
9 
The third adjustment relates to Service Company bonus depreciation rates.  
10 
The 100 percent bonus depreciation until January 1, 2023, is not available for 
11 
Service Company.  Under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, the deductibility of 100 
12 
percent bonus depreciation is tied to the interest expense limitations under 
13 
Section 163(j) of the Internal Revenue Code.  National Grid’s classification as 
14 
a regulated public utility for Section 163(j) is determined on a consolidated 
15 
tax return basis.  If 90 percent of the tax basis of National Grid’s assets in all 
16 
companies are within those subsidiaries classified as public utilities, National 
17 
Grid is not subject to the interest expense disallowance.  Because National 
18 
Grid falls within that threshold, the 100 percent bonus depreciation rate is not 
19 
available for any company included in the consolidated federal income tax 
20 
return, including Service Company.  
21 


--- Page 12 ---
 
Corrections and Updates Testimony of The Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 10 of 40

4

5

3 
Q. 
Does the Company have any updates to its forecast for Facilities 
4 
investments? 
5 
A.     Yes.  In the Company’s July 31 filing, the Company’s forecast of indirect 
6 
capital costs included the estimated costs associated with the planned lease of 
7 
a new Long Island office space to replace the existing Hicksville office 
8 
facility on Long Island.  As explained in the Company’s response to 
9 
Information Request No. DPS-711, in recognition of the impact of the 
10 
COVID-19 pandemic on National Grid’s operations and customers, National 
11 
Grid reevaluated its approach for the Long Island facilities and will instead 
12 
invest in upgrading the existing office spaces and parking infrastructure to 
13 
accommodate its employees.  National Grid believes that, with the appropriate 
14 
modifications, the existing facility can meet employee needs and will still 
15 
allow for the efficiency and productivity of employees for the benefit of 
16 
customers.  Although National Grid’s plans for the Long Island office are 
17 
preliminary, initial projections indicate that the projected spending to upgrade 
18 
the existing space aligns with National Grid’s initial projects for the lease and 
19 
therefore the forecast spending allocated to Niagara Mohawk has not been 
20 
updated.   
21

Authority (“NYPA”) (Segment A) and Transco (Segment B).  To facilitate 
5 
that use, the Company and developers needed to execute agreements to sell 
6 
certain transmission assets as well as allow for the use of existing Company 
7 
transmission corridors.  Recently, the Company executed agreements with LS 
8 
Power and NYPA, and anticipates executing an agreement with Transco by 
9 
the end of this month, and therefore provides an update on the projects herein.    
10 
 
11 
Q. 
Please explain the relevant terms of those agreements. 
12 
A. 
With respect to the Segment A project, LS Power has agreed to a purchase 
13 
price of $20.445 million for the physical assets, and LS Power and NYPA 
14 
have agreed to $31.051 million for a 99-year ground lease of approximately 
15 
93 miles of the Company’s transmission corridor.  The lease and asset 
16 
purchase agreement were filed for Commission approval under Public Service 
17 
Law Section 70 in Case 20-E-0491.  Transco will also execute a 99-year 
18 
ground lease for approximately 54 miles of the Company’s transmission 
19 
corridor and purchase $6.912 million of physical assets for the Segment B 
20 
project.  For both segments, the timing of the lease of land is anticipated to 
21 


--- Page 40 ---
 
Corrections and Updates Testimony of The Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 38 of 40 
 
occur once the Section 70 petitions are approved; however, the timing of the 
1 
asset transfers are expected to occur over a period of time and in a series of 
2 
transfers commensurate with the developers’ project schedules. 
3 
 
4 
Q. 
How does the Company propose to treat the proceeds of the transactions? 
5 
A. 
The Company proposed specific accounting treatment in the Section 70 
6 
petition filed with the Commission in Case 20-E-0491 and will propose the 
7 
same accounting in the forthcoming joint Section 70 petition with Transco.  
8 
The proposed accounting will be reviewed and approved by the Commission 
9 
in that case.  At a high level, the Company proposes to place all proceeds 
10 
received under the lease and asset purchase agreements into separate interest 
11 
bearing Other Deferred Credit – FERC 253 accounts for future return to 
12 
customers after the conclusion of all applicable regulatory review periods, 
13 
including those before the Commission, FERC, and the NYISO, which are 
14 
anticipated to conclude in June 2024.  Given the timing associated with the 
15 
closure of applicable regulatory review periods, the Company will propose the 
16 
return of the asset sales deferral created for this transaction in its next rate 
17 
filing, as well the amortized lease revenues.  The land lease deferral, however, 
18 
will begin to be reclassified as revenue monthly over the 99-year lease term, 
19 
with the majority of the balance remaining in the deferred credit account prior 
20 
to the Company’s next rate filing.     
21 


--- Page 41 ---
 
Corrections and Updates Testimony of The Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 39 of 40 
 
 
1 
Q. 
What mechanism does the Company propose to use to return these 
2 
transaction proceeds to customers in the future? 
3 
A. 
The physical asset sale proceeds will be accounted for as salvage in the 
4 
Accumulated Depreciation Reserve – FERC account 108, thereby reducing 
5 
rate base in the Company’s next rate case.  The lease proceeds will be 
6 
reclassified as Rent from Electric Property – FERC 454 account over the 99-
7 
year lease term.  As discussed in the corrections and updates testimony of the 
8 
Company’s Electric Rate Design Panel, the Company proposes to modify the 
9 
transmission revenue adjustment (“TRAC”) mechanism to return the proceeds 
10 
of the land lease to customers as booked to revenue.  The interest accrued on 
11 
both deferred credit accounts will be reclassified to a Regulatory Liability – 
12 
FERC 254 account at the closure of applicable regulatory review periods for 
13 
future pass back to customers. 
14 
 
15 
Q. 
Are there additional AC Proceeding Projects being included in the 
16 
Company’s Corrections and Updates? 
17 
A. 
Yes, as discussed in the EIOP’s corrections and updates testimony, the 
18 
Company is including two Segment A projects for the Edic Substation 
19 
Upgrade and the Line 30 Reconductoring Project in the net utility plant 
20 


--- Page 42 ---
 
Corrections and Updates Testimony of The Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 40 of 40 
 
forecast presented in Exhibit ___ (RRP-7), Schedule 1.  The associated 
1 
operating expense was included in Exhibit ___  (RRP-3), Schedule 27. 
2 
 
3 
Q. 
How does the Company propose to recover the costs of the Edic 
4 
Substation Upgrade and Line 30 Reconductoring Project? 
5 
A. 
The costs of these upgrades will be allocated to the beneficiaries of the 
6 
Segment A project.  The Company proposes to model the capital, O&M, and 
7 
offsetting revenue components of its revenue requirement in a manner 
8 
consistent with the ratemaking treatment proposed for the Western New York 
9 
Public Policy Transmission Needs Project in our direct testimony.    
10 
 
11 
XII. 
Conclusion 
12 
Q. 
Does this conclude the Panel’s testimony? 
13 
A. 
Yes, it does.

NIAGARA MOHAWK POWER CORPORATION d/b/a NATIONAL GRID 
Case Nos. 20-E-0380 and 20-G-0381 
Electric and Gas Rates 
Request for Information 
FROM: 
DPS Staff, Anthony DiGiacomo 
TO: 
National Grid, Revenue Requirements & Electric Infrastructure and Operations 
Panels 
SUBJECT:  
Storm Fund 
Request: 
Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
Pages 116-118 of the Electric Infrastructure & Operations Panel discusses the Company’s 
proposal to implement a two-way reconciliation mechanism for minor storm costs. 
1.
What specific rate allowance does NMPC propose to reconcile the minor storm costs
around?
2.
For calendar years 2010 through 2019, provide the supporting documentation behind
minor storm costs broken out by each storm event.  This should include, but not be
limited to, expenses broken down by incremental and base costs, by the different cost
components, and number of customers interrupted.
3.
Provide the Company’s rationale and supporting data behind the $10 million deadband.
4.
Provide all accounting and training procedures in place to prevent NMPC employees
from inaccurately charging minor storm work time as non-storm work time or vice versa.
Response:  
1.
See Attachment 1 for the detail by cost element of Historic Test Year (HTY) minor storm
costs inflated to the Rate Year.  The total Rate Year allowance for minor storm expense
included in the Company’s filing is $32.683 million as presented on Attachment 1, and is
the amount that the Company proposes to reconcile around, using a $10 million dead
band as described in the testimony of the Electric Infrastructure and Operations Panel.
This $32.683 million minor storm allowance is predicated on adoption of the Company’s
Exhibit______(RRP-11CU)
Workpapers to Exhibit RRP-3CU 
Schedule 2
Workpaper 9
Page 1 of 2


--- Page 549 ---
Form 103 
proposal to align the definition of a deferrable major storm with the definition used for 
reliability purposes, as discussed in the Company’s response to DPS-524.  If the major 
storm definition change is not adopted, the minor storm expense allowance should 
increase to $58.815 million to include the costs associated with storms that are major 
based on the reliability definition but not deferrable based on the current definition of a 
deferrable major storm.  The analysis for this response resulted in a recategorization of 
$4.011 million in costs associated with the 12/29/2019 major storm event that were 
included in minor storm costs in the Company’s initial filing and moved to major 
deferrable and major non-deferrable storm costs.  The work paper supporting the HTY 
adjustments to remove deferrable major storm costs provided in Exhibit___(RRP-3), 
Schedules 2 will be updated accordingly in the Company’s correction and updates filing. 
2.
The Company does not maintain or have readily available statistics on customer outages
that are linked to minor storms.  Minor storms are not defined by events, but, rather are
any weather-caused outages not meeting the criteria of a major storm event.  Minor storm
costs are recorded on the Company’s general ledger to one work order per division per
month and not associated with any specific event.  Attachment 2 presents minor storm
costs incurred by the Company broken down by base and incremental, and by cost
element.  As discussed with Staff, in Case 17-E-0238 the Company provided cost
information from calendar year 2013 and forward because of challenges obtaining pre-
2013 information due to moving from a legacy general ledger system to the SAP system.
If Staff advises the Company that data prior to 2013 is needed for this response, the
Company will determine what information can be provided and the estimated timeframe
for doing so.

SUBJECT:   Other Expense 
Note: In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall be 
construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet models in original 
electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
Referring to Exhibit__(RRP-11), Workpapers to Exhibit RRP-3, Schedule 7, Workpaper 1, page 
13, the Company includes $326,055 of costs related to Gridforce One Time Vendor. 
1.
Provide copies of all the invoices that support the costs related to Gridforce One Time
Vendor in the amount of $326,055.
2.
Provide the actual accounting applied (e.g., originating company, receiving order,
purchase order number, allocation code, allocation percent to NMPC electric and gas,
allocation methodology) so that verification of costs incurred can be reconciled with the
Historic Test Year workpapers provided in Exhibit__(RRP-11).
3.
Explain the nature of these costs and why the Company incurred them.
4.
Provide copies of the purchase orders that support and identify the work being performed.
5.
Explain whether or not these costs will recur during the Rate Year.
Response:  
1-5. 
The line items with the vendor text “Gridforce One Time Vendor” are Company
payments for residential gas conversions.  These payments were reclassed to 
Exhibit__(RRP-3), Schedule 38, and subsequently normalized from the Historic Test 
Year.  While the reclass took place on Exhibit__(RRP-3), Schedule 38 in the Company’s 
original filing, the corresponding normalization adjustment to Exhibit__(RRP-3), 
Schedule 7 will be reflected in the Company’s Corrections and Updates filing.  The 
Company is not seeking recovery of these charges.

DPS Staff, Michael Summa 
TO: 
 
National Grid, Revenue Requirement Panel 
SUBJECT:   Service Company Rent Expense
Request: 
Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
Referring to Exhibit__(RRP-11), Workpapers to Exhibit__(RRP-3) Schedule 9, Workpaper 11, 
the Company uses a long-term debt cost rate of 4.29% in the capital structure to develop the 
Service Company Rent Expense.  However, on page 24 of the Direct Testimony of the Capital 
Structure Panel, the Panel uses a long-term debt cost rate of 3.25% in the capital structure to 
develop the Service Company Rent Expense. 
1.
Confirm that the long-term debt cost rate used in the capital structure to develop the 
Service Company Rent Expense needs to be updated from 4.29% to 3.25%.  If not, 
explain why it does not need to be updated. 
2.
Provide the impact to the electric and gas revenue requirements of updating the long-term 
debt cost rate in the capital structure used to develop the Service Company Rent Expense 
from 4.29% to 3.25%. 
3.
Provide the workpapers and documentation to support the updated long-term debt cost 
rate of 3.25%. 
Response:  
1.
The Company agrees that the Long-Term Debt Cost rate needs to be updated from 4.29% 
to 3.25% in the Service Company Expense Rent models to correctly align with the 
Capital Structure Panel. 
2.  
Please see Attachment 1 for the calculated impact to the electric and gas Service 
Company Expense Rent revenue requirements as a result of updating the Long-Term 
Debt Cost rate from 4.29% to 3.25%. 
Exhibit______(RRP-11CU)
Workpapers to Exhibit RRP-3CU

3.  
Please see Attachment 2 for the workpaper used to support the updated Long-Term Debt 
Cost rate of 3.25%.  The Service Company data used for the calculation of the Long 
Term Debt Cost rate can also be found within the Capital Structure Panel’s direct 
testimony (see footnote on Page 24).

Request for Information 
FROM: 
DPS Staff, Michael Summa 
TO: 
 
National Grid, Revenue Requirements Panel 
SUBJECT:   Service Company Rent Expense 
Request: 
Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
Referring to the Excel file “RRP-3 OM Sch 9 SC Rents”, WP-4 Facilities RY22 tab, for each of 
the facilities investments listed below, provide the following information: documentation to 
support the investment (i.e., whitepaper, sanction paper, or lease agreement), an explanation and 
support for the amortization period used, and an explanation and support for the bill pool used.  
Investment Name 
- 
Long Island Office 
- 
Brooklyn – Asset Replacement 
- 
Brooklyn Office 
- 
Res Woods Capital 
- 
Res Woods SWS Project 
- 
Res Woods Project Space 
Response:  
Please see Attachments 1-3 for documentation supporting the Brooklyn Office and Reservoir 
Woods investments. 
In recognition of the impact of COVID-19 on the Company’s operations and customers, the 
Company has reevaluated its initial approach to lease a new third-party space (Long Island 
Office) and will instead consolidate office-based employees within the existing footprint. The 
Company still anticipates investing the planned CAPEX dollars from this investment to 
adequately upgrade the aged infrastructure at existing sites and provide parking infrastructure. 
As the Company is still in the early stages of detailed planning for a return to work post vaccine, 
operations organizations are working to re-evaluate their needs for sites in light of the pandemic and 
Exhibit______(RRP-11CU)
Workpapers to Exhibit RRP-3CU 
Schedule 9
Workpaper 15
Page 4 of 6


--- Page 622 ---
Form 103  
new ways of working. At this time, the Company’s plans for the Long Island Office are 
preliminary and will continue to be updated over the next few months.
The Brooklyn Asset Replacement projects do not have any formal white papers or sanctioning 
documentation as the CAPEX costs are related to general standard and recurring improvements 
and maintenance work within the portion of the space of the MetroTech facility that the 
Company will be retaining.
The amortization periods are specific to each type of asset (Utility Accounts 390-399) and 
applied based on the useful life of a particular asset type. To be consistent with the amortization 
periods previously assigned for these types of assets (390- Structures and Improvements), the 
amortization period of 18 years (216 months) was utilized. Because these specific investments 
are for leasehold improvements (changes to rental property), the Company believes it would be 
more appropriate to amortize these improvements over the life of the 15-year lease (180 months) 
and will make the update in the correction and updates filing. 
For the Bill Pool (Allocations) used for each investment, the Company evaluates which 
companies will benefit from the investments once placed into service. For the Long Island and 
Brooklyn offices, Hicksville Transportation Building (J-137) and Metrotech (J-139) allocation 
codes were used, as those allocation codes would most closely approximate the future occupancy 
of the new footprint. Please note that the J-137 allocation was incorrectly applied for the Long 
Island Property Strategy investment in the Company’s original filing and will be adjusted to 
Hicksville Main Office Building (J-127) in corrections and updates.  For the Brooklyn Asset 
Replacement investments, a Metrotech (J-139) (Facilities Allocation) was used as these 
investments would be directly improving and maintaining the Metrotech Facility.  For the 
Reservoir Woods investments, a Reservoir Woods (J-063) (Facilities Allocation) was used as 
that would be the most appropriate allocation of these costs given the relation directly to the 
usage of the actual site.  Attachment 4 presents the J Allocation codes used.

NOTES
Notes on Property/Terrorism/Business Interruption Charges to NMP and LIPA
1. NM Properties (NMP) is charged a share of the Property & Terrorism premiums for its coverage under these policies.
2. LIPA is charged a share of the Property, Terrorism & Business Interruption premiums for its lease of space at several NG facilities.
1. Insurance premiums are allocated using the SAP allocation code that most closely mirrors the underlying exposures that are being insured. If an appropriate SAP allocation code is not available, the insurance premiums are allocated manually.
2. For example, the Workers Compensation, Fidelity Bond (Crime), Employment Practices Liability, and Fiduciary insurance policies have a common risk exposure – the number of employees. An all-company SAP allocation code, which is based on the number of employees, is used to allocate the
premiums to all companies covered under these policies.
3. The Property and Property Terrorism insurance premiums are based on the replacement value of the property insured and associated prior loss history. There is no predefined SAP allocation code that fits this risk exposure profile. Therefore, the insurance premiums are manually allocated to all
companies covered under these policies based on insurable values and loss history.
3. Property valuation methodology changed from 80% value/20% loss history for 2018-2019 renewal to 100% value/00% loss history for 2019-2020 renewal. This explains the substantial allocation increase for electric segment.
4. For forecast for FY22 - FY24, tailored % increase as applied rather than 2% inflation index cross the board. Given the hardening state of the insurance market and the feedback received from insurers, the rate increase will be more than 2%. Rate increase will be varied but some lines will have

National Grid, Revenue Requirements Panel 
SUBJECT:   Other Initiatives - FTEs 
Request: 
Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
According to the MS Excel workpapers “RRP-3 Sch 27 Other Initiatives NM", specifically tab 
“Input #1 – FTEs,” the Company is including the costs associated with a pension plan for each of 
the incremental FTEs the Company plans on hiring by the end of the Rate Year.  Since NMPC’s 
pension plans are closed to newly hired employees, explain why these costs are included in the 
Rate Year forecast. 
Response:  
As discussed in the direct testimony of Company Witness Maureen Heaphy, new members of 
Local 97 are eligible for a pension plan.  New management employees and new members of 
Local 97C are not eligible for a pension but are eligible for a defined contribution plan, or 
enhanced thrift.  Therefore, the calculation of costs for Local 97 related incremental full-time 
equivalents (“FTE”) in Exhibit ___ (RRP-3), Schedule 27 correctly includes pension costs.  The 
Company agrees that the costs for management and Local 97C incremental FTEs in Exhibit ___ 
(RRP-3), Schedule 27 should not have pension costs.  Because these management and Local 97C 
positions are eligible for an enhanced thrift benefit, which for new employees is 4% of base pay, 
the associated thrift overhead applied to these FTEs should be increased to reflect this 
enhancement.  By changing the current calculation of FTE costs to account for the pension and 
thrift eligibility previously discussed, costs would shift from pensions to thrift.  The current 
pension overhead rate used in the FTE calculation is 2.5%. An appropriate increase in the thrift 
overhead rate to account for the enhanced thrift benefit would approximate the pension rate but 
likely be slightly higher.  In its corrections and updates filing, the Company will eliminate 
pension costs from the calculation of management and Local 97C FTE costs and increase the 
thrift overhead rate by 2.5% for those same FTEs, thereby keeping the total revenue requirement 
unchanged but shifting costs from pensions to thrift.

be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet

Referring to Exhibit___(RRP-11), Workpapers to Exhibit RRP-3, Schedule 27, Workpaper 2, as 
it should be updated to include the missing positions as requested in DPS-472, the Company 
plans on hiring additional full-time equivalent (FTE) employees by the end of the Rate Year.   
 
1. 
For each FTE, if the anticipated start date has already passed, state if the position is 
currently filled, and whether the position was filled internally or externally. 
 
2. 
For each of the positions that were filled, state the actual start date and the amount of 
days between the actual start date and the anticipated start date presented in the 
Company’s workpapers. 
 
3. 
For each position that has not been filled and the anticipated start date of the position has 
passed, explain why the position has not been filled. 
 
4. 
For any positions that have been hired internally, explain whether the Company has 
backfilled the vacated position. 
 
5. 
Provide monthly updates to Questions 1 through 4, above on an on-going basis.

DPS Staff, Sarah Keymel

National Grid, Revenue Requirements Panel 
SUBJECT:   Other Initiatives - FTEs 
Request: 
Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
Referring to Exhibit___(RRP-11), Workpapers to Exhibit RRP-3, Schedule 27, Workpaper 2, as 
it should be updated to include the missing positions as requested in DPS-472, and the Excel 
workpapers these figures are derived from: 
1.
For each of the incremental positions NMPC plans to fill by the end of the Rate Year, that 
are to be fully charged to NMPC, explain how the Company determined 100% of the 
position’s time should be charged to NMPC.  Provide all supporting documentation and 
calculations.   
2.
For each of the incremental positions NMPC plans to fill by the end of the Rate Year, that 
are to be partially charged to NMPC, explain how the Company determined the percent 
of a position’s time to be charged NMPC.  Provide all supporting documentation and 
calculations. 
3.
For each incremental position NMPC plans to fill by the end of the Rate Year, explain 
how the Company determined the percent of time charged to electric versus gas.  
4.
For each incremental position NMPC plans to fill by the end of the Rate Year, explain 
how the Company determined the percent of time charged to operating expense. 
5.
For each position for which the Company lists a low salary and an average salary, explain 
what these salaries represent and how they were derived. 
6.
Explain the Company’s reasoning for using the low to average midpoint salary for each 
position.

--- Page 795 ---
Form 103  
7.
For each incremental position NMPC plans to fill by the end of the Rate Year, identify 
whether the position is an entry level position, and how the Company made that 
determination. 
8.
For each incremental position NMPC plans to fill by the end of the Rate Year, identify 
whether the position is expected to be filled internally or externally, and how the 
Company made that determination. 
Response:  
1.
See Attachment 1 for the information requested in Parts 1 through 4 and Parts 7 and 8.  
The additional full-time equivalents (“FTE”) for legal and the EAP program, the 
removal of one RNG procurement program FTE, and the allocation rates changes for the 
pipeline safety stakeholder engagement FTE, the multi-use hydrogen FTE, and the first 
responder training FTEs, as discussed in the Company’s response to DPS-472, are 
reflected in Attachment 1.  A column titled “Corrections and Updates to Original Filing” 
in Attachment 1 indicates these and other changes that the Company will reflect in its 
corrections and updates filing.   
2.
See response to Part 1. 
3.
See response to Part 1. 
4.
See response to Part 1. 
5.
The salaries in the referenced Workpaper 2 are from payroll as of December 31, 2019, 
the end of the Historic Test Year.  Payroll for the operating company to which the FTE 
is assigned is used to determine the salary for the FTE’s job title.  If payroll for that 
operating company does not have the job title, then the job title in Service Company 
payroll is used to determine the salary for the job title.  The final salary used in 
calculating the cost associated with the FTE is the midpoint between the lowest and 
average salary on payroll for the job title. 
6.
FTE positions can be filled by candidates with varying levels of experience and thus at 
varying levels of starting salary.  Using the mid-point between the lowest salary on 
payroll and average salary on payroll is a conservative approach to determine a salary 
that accounts for this variability.  Also, this method of determining salary has been 
consistently used and accepted by Staff in National Grid’s previous four New York rate 
cases. 
7.
See response to Part 1.

MECOD, NECOD,
NIMOD
Develop a tool and process to better manage a book shelf of ready to work
projects, to avoid writing off the work that has been designed. Preparation to
have right work in right locations. Initiative ensures work availability in
advance 8-10 weeks. 1) ensures crew productivity can be maintained by having

unforeseen delays on a current project and 2) reduces risk of designed projects
becoming stale and potentially cancelled after design activities completed.
Cancel ~$1M in projects a year typically.

start slow and increase from quarter to quarter due to new process being rolled
out and becoming standard.

701 Use remote sensors to optimize PM costs
IL5 (Realised)
37
0
0
37
Partial
Electric - Distribution
NIMOD
Install sensors just outside substations at feeder heads to reduce the need to
conduct manual operations. All tracking will be based on planned sensor
installations in NY and NE over the next 3 fiscal years on non EMS stations at
the feeder head. Manual operations analyzed include TOA based feeder head
load readings, readings of analog station load to obtain summer peak load
readings or for regular V&O inspections, and false positive station outages due
to single phase outages. To measure reduced OPEX it will be assumed that
sensors will make the previously defined manual operation unnecessary; the
calculation will be done using NY and NE data sets (where available and
relevant) to produce system averages of number of hours spent per year per
feeder on each operation, which will in turn inform an approximate amount of
OPEX that can potentially be avoided (on a per sensor basis).

15500 PiPro Data Analysis Efficiency
IL5 (Realised)
45
0
0
45
Yes - C
Electric - Distribution
NIMOD
PiPro is a software analysis tool (developed in python by DPAM) designed to
automate the analysis of load readings out of Pi. Specifically, the tool
automates the 'scrubbing' of the loading data, meaning it removes anomalies in
the data (such as switching peaks and minimums, meter failure, etc.). This is
normally manually performed by planning engineers, so the implementation of
this tool is anticipated to deliver savings in terms of employee hours. Some
assumptions are being made for the sake of forecasting efficiencies and savings
around management hourly wages, and time required to perform data analysis
tasks.

Request: 
Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
1. 
On page 92 of the Direct Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel, the Company 
proposes to amortize the costs to achieve over three years.  Referring to Exhibit__(RRP-
11), Workpapers to Exhibit RRP-3, Schedule 33, Workpaper 1, Page 2, it shows that the 
Company is amortizing the costs to achieve over four years.  Clarify the number of years 
the Company proposes to amortize the costs to achieve. 
2. 
On page 92 of the Direct Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel, the Company 
proposes to amortize the costs to achieve over three years.  Explain the reasoning for 
amortizing the costs to achieve amounts over three years (or four years depending on the 
Company’s response to question 1 above). 
3. 
On page 94 of the Direct Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel, the Company 
mentions the level of savings is increased by inflation in the Rate Year and each of the 
Data Years.  Referring to Exhibit__(RRP-3), Summary, Pages 3 and 4, the Company 
does not increase the Rate Year amount by inflation.  Clarify the Company’s position on 
whether the savings are intended to be increased by inflation in the Rate Year and each of 
the Data Years. 
Response:  
1. The Company proposes to amortize the costs to achieve over three years, matching the term 
of the proposed rate plan.  The four years referenced in Exhibit__(RRP-11), Workpapers to 
Exhibit RRP-3, Schedule 33 is incorrect and will be corrected in Corrections and Updates. 
Exhibit______(RRP-11CU)
Workpapers to Exhibit RRP-3CU 
Schedule 33
Workpaper 4
Page 1 of 2


--- Page 898 ---
Form 103  
2. The costs to achieve were incurred by the Company to deliver the forecast savings in the 
Rate Year and Data Years.  The Company amortized the costs to achieve over three years to 
align with the benefits that the Company is proposing to reflect for customers over the same 
period. 
3. The Company inadvertently excluded the inflation rate from the Rate and Data Year 
calculations.  The Company will make this correction in Corrections and Updates.

Rate Case Expense 
Request: 
Note: 
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
Referring to Exhibit__(RRP-11), Schedule 29, Workpaper 2, page 1 of 1, provide the work 
activities for each consultant listed and the calculations underlying the forecasted amounts for 
each consultant. 
Response:  
Please see Attachment 2 for the updated Foster Associates forecast.  Please see Attachments 3 
and 4 for rate case (i) public hearing publication costs (“Hearing Publication”) and (ii) rate 
publication (“Rate Publication”) costs incurred to date, respectively (collectively, “Publication 
Costs”).   
The Rate Publication costs in Attachment 4 of $100,449 serve as the basis for Rate Publication 
costs each year.  Rate Publications are required when the Company files a rate case as well as 
each time rates change as part of a rate plan.  Assuming a three-year rate plan, Rate Publication 
costs will be incurred a total of four times throughout the rate filing (i.e., once after the initial 
filing, once when rates are approved by the Commission, once before the start of the second rate 
year, and a final time before the start of the third rate year).  Hearing Publication costs occur one 
time at the request of the Administrative Law Judges to provide the public with notice of the 
upcoming public statement hearings in a rate proceeding.  When the four Rate Publication costs 
are summed with the Hearing Publication costs in Attachment 3, the result is the total forecast 
for Publication Costs of $479,453. 
The Company’s Corrections and Updates filing will reflect the incremental $0.030 million gas 
expense per year for the updated Foster Associates forecast and the incremental $0.080 million 
of Publication Costs per year in both electric and gas expense.  Additionally, in the Historic Test

costs.  The Company will make a normalization adjustment in Corrections and Updates to

Please note that Attachment 2 contains confidential vendor pricing information.  Both a redacted

SUBJECT:   Storm Fund 
 
Request: 
 
 
Note: 
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
 
Exhibit_(RRP-11), Workpapers to Exhibit_(RRP-3), Schedule 38, Workpaper 1 lists the 
Incremental Major Storm Costs. 
 
1. 
Provide a breakout showing each storm event included in the “Major Non-Deferrable” 
column for each year. 
 
2. 
For each storm identified in question 1, provide a breakout of the expenses broken down 
by base and incremental, and by the different cost components. 
 
3. 
For each storm identified in question 1, provide the total number of customers in each 
region, number of customers interrupted, and number of customers interrupted for 24 
hours. 
 
4. 
Does NMPC agree that DPS Staff audits of major deferrable storm events and their 
associated adjustments should be accounted for in the Storm Fund forecast? 
 
5. 
Provide the major storm events for calendar year 2018. 
 
6. 
Provide the major storm events for calendar year 2019. 
 
7. 
For each major storm identified in response to question 6, provide a breakout of the 
expenses broken down by base and incremental, and by the different cost components.

Response:  
 
1. 
See Attachment 1 for the major non-deferrable storms represented in Exhibit___(RRP-
11), Workpapers to Exhibit___(RRP-3), Schedule 41, Workpaper 1.  In putting together 
this response the Company determined revisions were necessary to this workpaper for 
three reasons; first, incorrect amounts were inadvertently transferred to the schedule for 
major non-deferrable storm events; second, major deferrable storm costs were updated to 
reflect adjustments agreed to by the Company resulting from Staff’s major storm audit; 
and third, the $400,000 threshold was applied to the storm events.  See Attachment 2 for 
a revised Exhibit___(RRP-11), Workpapers to Exhibit___(RRP-3), Schedule 41, 
Workpaper 1 that will be included in the Company’s Corrections and Updates filing. 
  
2. 
See Attachment 1 for the detailed costs for major non-deferrable storms as requested.

SUBJECT:   Storm Fund
Request: 
Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
1.
Explain if the figures for each major storm event listed in Exhibit_(RRP-11), 
Workpapers to Exhibit_(RRP-3), Schedule 41, Workpaper 1, follow all the “Major 
Storm Expense Provisions” included in Appendix 14 of the Joint Proposal adopted by 
the Commission in Cases 17-E-0238 and 17-G-0239, e.g., contractor disallowance, 
service company exclusions, etc. 
2.
As a follow-up question to DPS-523 question 1, explain if the amounts for each “Major 
Non-Deferrable” storm event follow the “Major Storm Expense Provisions” provided in 
Appendix 14 of the Joint Proposal adopted by the Commission in Cases 17-E-0238 and 
17-G-0239, with the exception of what qualifies as a major storm.  If not, provide the 
incremental amount for each storm event if the “Major Storm Expense Provisions” were 
followed. 
Response:  
1.
See the Company’s response to DPS-523 for a revised version of Exhibit_(RRP-11), 
Workpapers to Exhibit_(RRP-3), Schedule 41, Workpaper 1 that will be included in the 
Company’s Corrections and Updates filing.  The major storm expenses on that workpaper, 
as noted, reflect disallowances and exclusions in accordance with Appendix 14 of the Joint 
Proposal in Case 17-E-0238 (“Storm Provision”), as well as audit adjustments previously 
agreed to by the Company and Staff during Staff’s major storm deferral audit.  
Additionally, because the review of costs and the calculation of all exclusions to the major 
deferrable storm costs for calendar years 2018 and 2019 events are not final, the costs in 
Schedule 41, Workpaper 1 for those years reflect only contractor, consultant, and overtime 
Exhibit______(RRP-11CU)
Workpapers to Exhibit RRP-3CU 
Schedule 41
Workpaper 1
Page 17 of 18


--- Page 924 ---
Form 103  
costs (i.e., the costs exclude affiliate base labor and transportation, employee expenses, 
materials and other expenses) as an approximation of the total incremental costs after 
disallowances and exclusions. 
2.
The major non-deferrable storm costs presented in the revised version of Exhibit_(RRP-
11), Workpapers to Exhibit_(RRP-3), Schedule 41, Workpaper 1 provided in the 
Company’s response to DPS-523 include only incremental storm costs as defined by cost 
element, consistent with the Storm Provision.  The costs also reflect the following 
adjustments consistent with the Storm Provision: 
i. 
application of the $400,000 per storm threshold, limited to $800,000 per year 
ii. 
an estimate of 6% of incremental costs as disallowances and exclusions (payroll 
tax on overtime, invoice scrubbing, Service Co. exclusion) based on the rate of 
disallowances and exclusions determined for major deferrable storms in calendar 
years 2016 and 2017. 
Schedule 41, Workpaper 1 presents incremental storm costs over the past ten years and 
calculates the annual average amount for purposes of setting a reconciling major storm 
expense allowance.  The Company believes that the adjustments described above in Parts 
1 and 2, applied to both major deferrable and non-deferrable storm costs in Schedule 41, 
Workpaper 1 provided in response to DPS-523, provide a reasonable allowance for this 
purpose, equal to approximately $31 million.
